newsitem.title: UK: Resistant bacteria widespread in hospitals - study.
newsitem.headline: Resistant bacteria widespread in hospitals - study.

text.p: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria are more common in hospitals than was feared and can quietly spread from patient to patient despite strict hygiene, researchers reported on Friday.

A survey in Chicago's Cook County Hospital found that vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) -- a type of gut bacteria that resists the antibiotic most commonly used against it -- was widespread both in patients and on equipment such as beds.
Marc Bonten and colleagues tested 92 patients for the bacteria who were on ventilators (respirators) between April and May 1995, and also took cultures all around the hospital.
More than 40 percent of patients became colonised with the bacteria while in hospital. Another 24 percent came into the hospital already carrying the bacteria.
"VRE colonisation was persistent in 20 of the 21 ventilated patients," they wrote in the Lancet medical journal. "Six of these patients harboured more than one strain type of VRE."
Sixteen of the patients became infected by the bacteria, although because they were so ill anyway it was hard to isolate their symptoms. None died.
"Most had abdominal infections," Bonten said in a telephone interview. "Some had urine cultures, indicating they had bladder infections."
Bonten's group found that patients who had been given vancomycin or similar antibiotics before were more likely to become infected. This had also been found in previous studies.

Antibiotic-resistant bacteria are dangerous to patients who are very ill or those who have their immune systems damped down -- for instance, organ transplant or leukaemia patients. Usually they can be dealt with by switching to a new antibiotic, but VRE is proving harder to kill and doctors are testing new drugs.
Most people carry bacteria with no symptoms at all.
Bonten's team found careful precautions were not enough to stop the bacteria from spreading. Despite careful use of gloves and disinfectant, bacteria were found in the rooms of 13 patients.
"VRE have also been shown to persist on gloved and ungloved hands for at least 60 minutes," Bonten, now at University Hospital Maastricht in the Netherlands, wrote.

They recommended that all patients admitted to intensive care units be screened for the bacteria, and said the spread had been stopped in some cases with "aggressive" measures that included isolating contaminated patients.

Antibiotic-resistant bacteria and fungi are a big threat in hospitals. Many forms have evolved that resist several different types of antibiotic and doctors fear a form will eventually arise than cannot be killed by anything.
Last week a British doctor reported that VRE had mutated even further, into a form that actually depended on vancomycin for its survival. (c) Reuters Limited 1996
